turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not astonished, I confess, at your knowing little of his misfortunes, or I might rather say, of his real character. Your want of concern for him was enough to betray you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am well aware that my actions have been misconstrued, but I must defend myself against such accusations. My treatment of Mr. Wickham has been a matter of principle and not of malice.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your actions may have been a matter of principle, but they have also been a matter of pride, Mr. Darcy. Your treatment of Mr. Wickham has not been without fault.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I have indeed been guided by my pride, but also by a sense of duty and honour that you, Miss Bennet, may not fully comprehend.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your sense of duty and honour seem to have blinded you to the pain you have caused, Mr. Darcy. How can you expect me to believe that your actions were not motivated by malice when they have hurt so many?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: My actions may have been perceived as harsh, Miss Bennet, but I assure you they were not intended to cause malice or unnecessary pain. I have always acted within the confines of what I deemed necessary and proper.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your actions may be within your confines of propriety, Mr. Darcy, but they have certainly not been within the hearts and minds of those you have wronged.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware of the perception of my actions, Miss Bennet, but I must defend my character and intentions. My conduct, however misguided, was not borne of malice but of a misguided sense of duty.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your misguided sense of duty, Mr. Darcy, has caused considerable harm and hurt. It is not enough to merely say your intentions were good if your actions have such negative consequences.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand your criticism, Miss Bennet, and I shall endeavour to make amends for my past errors. Yet, I must also defend myself against unfounded accusations and the misunderstanding of my intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may defend your character and intentions all you like, Mr. Darcy, but until you have shown me through your actions that you have changed, it will be difficult for me to believe anything but what I have seen.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand your skepticism and the weight of your disapproval. It is not within my nature to change overnight, but I assure you, I am committed to altering my ways and earning your regard.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I see your commitment, Mr. Darcy, but actions truly do speak louder than words. Prove to me that you are a different man, and then we can revisit this conversation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words cut deep, but I shall use this pain to guide my transformation. I will act with sincerity and humility, ensuring my actions align with my intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I appreciate your words, Mr. Darcy, and I hope that your intentions are true. But as I said before, your actions will determine the course of my opinion.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I shall do as you bid, Miss Bennet, and prove my sincerity through my deeds. Until then, I must endure your displeasure and the scrutiny of your judgment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Well, Mr. Darcy, I shall await the demonstration of your change. Until then, there is little else to be said.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your judgment, Miss Bennet, shall be my compass. I shall endeavor to earn your regard through my actions alone.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I see, Mr. Darcy. Your words are grand, but remember, actions speak louder than words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand your sentiments. I shall leave you now and give you the space to reflect on my words. May your thoughts be as fair as your judgment.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
